strengths: Thorough empirical evaluation with controlled hyperparameter sweeps across three large-scale datasets (60k-1M actions), demonstrating consistent improvements of PWLL over IPS-based methods
Clear and well-motivated core insight: optimization landscape matters as much or more than statistical properties of estimators, with effective toy example (Figure 1) illustrating the key difference
Rigorous theoretical analysis formalizing how optimization difficulty (plateaus, local maxima) scales with effective action space size K_eff (Propositions 2.1-2.2)
Systematic oracle policy analysis revealing implicit biases of different IPS estimators, providing clean mathematical characterization
Practical design principles (objective-aware parametrization, PWLL preference) that are actionable for practitioners
Comprehensive ablations covering noise robustness, hyperparameter sensitivity, cluster/support sensitivity, and comparison to pessimistic methods
Concavity guarantee for PWLL (Proposition 3.1) provides formal optimization advantages with convergence analysis (Appendix D)
Reproducibility ensured through code release and detailed experimental documentation
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Propositions 2.1-2.2 primarily adapt existing results from Chen et al. (2019) and Mei et al. (2020a); oracle policy analysis is standard expectation-taking; concavity of log-likelihood objectives is relatively straightforward

Theory-practice gap not adequately addressed: concavity guarantee (Prop 3.1) assumes linear softmax policies but experiments use inner-product policies; Remark 3.2 admits concavity is lost with end-to-end deep learning; oracle analysis assumes infinite data with no finite-sample guarantees

Claims 2.3-2.4 lack formal justification: no theorems or proofs establishing that restricting A_eff to S_0 preserves oracle optimality; no analysis of approximation error if true optimal policy has support outside S_0

Unclear PWLL positioning: paper claims PWLL is not novel (from offline RL), yet empirically it is central; distinction from advantage-weighted behavioral cloning insufficiently clarified; relationship to existing log-likelihood objectives in contextual bandits underexplored

Narrow experimental scope: all experiments on collaborative filtering only; no evaluation on other contextual bandit domains or applications; logging policy restriction (top k_0=100) already constrains action space, potentially confounding comparisons

PWLL limitations insufficiently explored: acknowledged inability to perform OPE/policy selection without solutions offered; oracle policies depend on logging coverage with no failure mode analysis; much higher MSE than IPS methods (Figure 3) with insufficient discussion of when this tradeoff is unacceptable; comparison to IPS not entirely fair as PWLL uses reward signals directly while IPS designed for evaluation

Experimental design concerns: reward model learned from same data introduces potential bias; no comparison to simpler baselines (behavior cloning); no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; Figure 2 difficult to interpret with overlapping lines

Incomplete analysis of design choices: implementation details missing (how is S_0 computed in practice?); sensitivity to k_0 not studied; Section 2.3 claim about MIPS/OffCEM/PC falling into trap needs more rigorous formalization
Convergence analysis in Appendix D provides only standard O(1/√T) rates for concave objectives and geometric rates for regularized case—not novel

strengths: Identifies important practical problem: optimization landscape difficulty in large action spaces is underexplored despite practical importance
Thorough empirical validation: three datasets (60k-1M actions), controlled optimization sweeps, multiple ablations with error bars and seeds
Solid theoretical analysis: Propositions 2.1-2.2 formalize how optimization pathologies scale with K_eff; Proposition 3.1 proves PWLL concavity; oracle policy framework provides actionable insights
Effective presentation: clear writing, well-designed figures (especially Figure 1 and 2), honest discussion of limitations and lack of novelty
Actionable guidance with practical impact: specific design rules (Claims 2.3-2.4) will influence real deployments in recommender systems
Rigorous experimental design: Figure 2's hyperparameter sensitivity analysis convincingly shows PWLL robustness vs IPS fragility across batch sizes and learning rate schedules
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: PWLL objectives (LPI, cLPI, RegKL) are known from offline RL literature; objective-aware parametrization (restricting to π₀'s support) is intuitive; concavity follows straightforwardly from log transformation

Theoretical analysis is worst-case rather than typical-case: Propositions 2.1-2.2 construct specific problem instances where pathologies occur but don't characterize when they arise in typical problems
Concavity guarantee restricted to linear-softmax policies: Proposition 3.1 doesn't hold for end-to-end deep network training, a significant practical limitation acknowledged only in Remark 3.2
Incomplete characterization of optimization-vs-estimation trade-off: no formal conditions stated for when optimization dominates; no problem-dependent convergence rates that account for OPL structure

Experimental concerns: (1) MSE comparison (Figure 3) unfairly characterizes PWLL as poor estimators when they target different objectives; (2) all experiments use inner-product policies—generalization to other parametrizations unclear; (3) hyperparameter tuning fairness not transparent; (4) simple linear regression for reward models
Claims 2.3-2.4 not formalized: no definition of what makes a parametrization 'compatible' or how practitioners should design compatible parametrizations for new estimators
Logging policy dependence underexplored: PWLL oracle policies depend on π₀'s coverage; impact on relative performance vs IPS-based methods not thoroughly characterized; relegated to appendix

Incomplete comparisons: Direct Method (DM) mentioned but not evaluated; limited engagement with other large-action-space approaches (hierarchical policies, action abstraction); recent methods cited but not compared
